summary: Defines tests for describing the performance of ATM switching devices, along with formats for reporting results. The goal is to let different devices be measured and compared in a consistent way.

eli5.summary: It is a rulebook for racing machines that move data, so every race is run the same way and results can be compared.

questions: how to test atm switch performance
subtitle: Standard tests and measurement procedures for ATM switch performance.

tldr.problem: ATM switches vary widely in capabilities and performance, making it hard for network operators to compare devices from different vendors using a consistent standard. Without agreed-upon tests, vendor claims cannot be directly compared.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3116 defines a suite of benchmarking tests from the IETF Benchmarking Methodology Working Group, specifying how to measure ATM switch performance across physical layer (SONET), ATM layer (cell delay, loss, errors), adaptation layer (AAL5), and signaling metrics. It describes test configurations, traffic patterns, and reporting formats so results are reproducible and comparable.
tldr.outcome: Network operators and procurement teams now have a standard methodology to benchmark ATM switches, allowing fair comparison of vendor products under consistent conditions. The tests help identify performance bottlenecks and validate that devices meet specified performance requirements.

facts.value: CDV, CER, CLR, CMR, CTD, CRC-ER

today: RFC 3116 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It remains the standard methodology for benchmarking ATM switches. While ATM usage in networks has declined in favor of IP-based technologies, RFC 3116 continues to be referenced in benchmarking of any remaining ATM infrastructure and has influenced benchmarking methodologies for modern networking technologies.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines a specific set of tests and procedures that vendors can use to measure and report the performance of ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) network devices. The methodology is based on RFC 2544, which did the same thing for general network interconnect devices, but adapted for ATM-specific measurements and configurations.

The document works alongside RFC 2761 ("Terminology for ATM Benchmarking"), which defines the terms; this RFC defines the procedures to measure them. Together they ensure that vendors and customers speak the same language and follow the same test protocols when comparing ATM switches.

RFC 3116 is a product of the IETF's Benchmarking Methodology Working Group, which focuses on creating standardized, reproducible test procedures. The group produces two types of documents: terminology documents that define metrics, and methodology documents (like this one) that explain how to collect those metrics.
sections.eli5: Think of this as the science fair rules: if you want to test which ATM switch is best, here's exactly how you set it up, what you measure, and how you report the results.

sections.title: Test Setup and Configuration
sections.content:
RFC 3116 prescribes specific test configurations. A uni-directional connection connects a test device's transmit port to one SUT (System Under Test) receive port and vice versa, measuring performance through one port pair. A bi-directional connection uses two port pairs on the same SUT to measure whether the device works correctly forwarding data between ports. A passthrough configuration chains multiple SUTs together to test end-to-end behavior.

Tests use specific IP PDU (Protocol Data Unit) sizes: 44, 64, 128, 256, 1024, 1518, 2048, 4472, and 9180 octets. These sizes range from minimal (to measure per-PDU overhead) to maximum (9180 octets is the ATM MTU). Tests must use actual traffic patterns: steady-state constant bit rate, variable bit rate (VBR) bursts, and mixed loads.

The SUT must be configured as it would be in production, with all supported protocols and features enabled. Test duration is at least 60 seconds for quick measurements or 300 seconds if results show high variance. All configuration details must be documented and reported.
sections.eli5: Set up the switch the way customers would use it, send real-world-like traffic patterns at it, and measure for long enough that the results are reliable.

sections.title: Performance Metrics: Three Layers of Testing
sections.content:
RFC 3116 organizes tests into three layers. Physical layer (SONET) tests measure how the switch handles line-level errors and timing issues. Tests check whether pointer movements (adjustments in SONET framing) or transport overhead (TOH) errors cause the switch to drop cells or packets. These tests verify that the switch is transparent to SONET-level signaling.

ATM layer tests measure the core ATM switching performance: Cell Delay Variation (CDV) measures how much variation there is in the time it takes a cell to traverse the switch; Cell Error Ratio (CER) measures how many cells arrive with bit errors; Cell Loss Ratio (CLR) measures how many cells are lost under load; Cell Misinsertion Rate (CMR) measures how many cells go to the wrong destination; and Cell Transfer Delay (CTD) measures latency. Each metric is tested under steady load, VBR bursts, and mixed load conditions, with varying numbers of Virtual Circuits (one VCC, twelve VCCs, or maximum supported).

Adaptation layer (AAL5) tests measure IP packet reassembly performance. At the IP level, the switch is supposed to be transparent; these tests verify that AAL5 reassembly works correctly even when cells are lost or corrupted.

A fourth set of tests covers ATM services: call setup time, connection teardown time, and signaling protocol performance.
sections.eli5: Tests work from the inside out: first check the electrical signals, then check cells, then check IP packets, then check whether establishing connections works correctly.

sections.title: Test Modifiers: Real-World Conditions
sections.content:
RFC 3116 specifies modifiers that tests can apply to create realistic conditions. Management traffic simulates SNMP or ILMI queries happening while the switch forwards data, testing whether management overhead impacts throughput. Routing updates simulate PNNI routing protocols running in the background, which can affect switch performance.

Filters test whether access control lists impact performance. Tests first use a single filter condition, then repeat with 25 filters to see how filter processing overhead scales. Multiple addresses test whether using random destination addresses (not just a single source-destination pair) affects performance.

Multi-port tests simulate realistic switching where multiple ports are used simultaneously, with each transmit port receiving identical distributions of PDUs from each receive port. This stresses the switch's forwarding fabric in ways that single-port tests do not.

The RFC emphasizes that tests should be run first without modifiers, then repeated under each modifier separately. All modifying PDUs must be part of the normal test stream, not supplied on a separate port.
sections.eli5: After testing the switch in clean conditions, add realistic complications: management queries, routing updates, firewall filters, and multiple ports all talking at once. The switch should still work, but might be slower.

sections.title: Reporting and Interpretation
sections.content:
Performing all recommended tests will generate large amounts of data. RFC 3116 emphasizes that the value of this data depends on understanding which tests apply to a particular SUT and what the results mean for the intended deployment. For example, ILMI timing measurements are not relevant for a WAN-only switch.

Results must be reported in specified table formats, with the exact traffic rate, PDU size, and test conditions documented. This allows readers to understand and reproduce the test. Critical information includes: the SUT version and exact configuration (what features were enabled or disabled), the IP PDU sizes used, the traffic rates tested, and the trial description.

The RFC warns that interpreting results requires understanding of testing practices regarding repeatability, variance, and statistical significance. A single test run may show random variation; multiple trials reduce variance. Test selection and evaluation should be done with knowledge of the network environment where the SUT will be deployed.
sections.eli5: You now have tons of numbers. Know which ones matter for your use case, repeat tests to make sure results are consistent, and understand that the same switch might perform differently in different networks.
